The study has as its objective 'to assess the magnitude of RM – as well as associated attitudes and factors – among faculty researchers conducting biomedical and epidemiological studies involving human participants in an academic institution in Ethiopia.'  The topic is important  especially in the context that it is the first of its kind in Ethiopia. Generally the manuscript is well written and the methods well described to make reproducibility of the study possible. However, the following issues /suggestions need to be addressed

1. Title.

I would suggest inserting 'a' in front of 'Public University.

2. Abstract

a) The aim of the study should be included either as a subheading or the second sentence in the Background subheading.

b) The conclusion has to be completely revised as I suggests below

3. Method

a) The variable 'Research experience' was measured by the number of years in an academic post. I wonder why the 'number of publications/scholarly works' was not used as a more appropriate marker for research experience?

4. Results

a) Table 2 is not in the manuscript.

b) Page 8- The sentence, 'A Chi-Square test showed significant associations with a p-value of less than 0.05'  has to be expanded to make it complete and self explanatory.

c) I suggest further analysis on Authorship misconduct should be provided to determine which of the 3 types studied was associated with more years of research experience.

The conclusion as stated does not derive from this particular study or related to the objective of the study as stated by the Authors. The conclusion is too generic and very broad without any specific link to either the results from this study or the stated objectives of the study. It should be completely re-written. In addition, since there was no significant difference in research misconduct between those that had prior training in ethics and those who did not, I wonder the basis for the recommendation of educational interventions in the conclusion

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm that it is of an acceptable scientific standard, however I have significant reservations, as outlined above.

Thank you for the opportunity to review this article. This cross-sectional study investigates the extent of research misconduct (RM) among researchers in Ethiopia’s academic and research institutions using a structured questionnaire. Some findings are particularly intriguing, such as the lack of significant statistical correlation between ethics education and RM. However, I have three primary concerns I would like to discuss with the authors.

Firstly, the authors examined behavioral influences on responsible conduct in research and explored factors associated with RM composites. While the selected factors appear relevant to RM, the authors do not delve deeply into why these factors may influence RM. This oversight may represent a limitation of the quantitative approach and raises questions for scholars engaged in qualitative research. Therefore, I recommend that the authors provide a more comprehensive explanation of these influencing factors, taking into account the educational and cultural context of Ethiopia, as well as relevant existing theories.

Secondly, as noted in the Discussion Sec., the findings from Ethiopia align with those from Kenya and the Middle East. Readers may be interested in understanding the uniqueness and broader applicability of this study. The research's distinctiveness should not be solely attributed to the choice of Ethiopia as the research site. This concern is related to my first point regarding the investigation of established factors influencing RM, as the significance of the research appears less pronounced. I suggest that the authors further explore the uniqueness of this study and its potential broader applicability in future research.

Thirdly, the article exhibits certain limitations in research methodology, particularly concerning the formulation of research hypotheses. The manuscript lacks a dedicated literature review section; instead, it briefly presents current research on RM in the Middle East within the Introduction Sec. This approach does not adequately develop research hypotheses by considering existing literature, which should be followed by validation through the questionnaire. I recommend that the authors enhance the methodological rigor of this cross-sectional study by incorporating a more thorough review of relevant literature to inform the formulation of their research hypotheses.

The manuscript by Ospanov and colleagues presents a case of a 38-year-old male with morbid obesity who underwent a laparoscopic one-anastomosis gastric bypass (OAGB) with a concomitant FundoRing procedure. The authors report the development of an acute obstruction at the gastrojejunal anastomosis on the first postoperative day, which they diagnose as “anastomositis.” The report details a successful outcome following a conservative, non-surgical treatment regimen. The patient’s symptoms of vomiting and belching resolved, and follow-up endoscopy confirmed a patent anastomosis, leading to discharge and significant weight loss at a three-month follow-up.

This case presents a novel instance of an early anastomotic complication managed successfully without invasive procedures. While the case itself is interesting and may contribute to the literature on bariatric surgery complications, the manuscript, in its current form, suffers from significant methodological and reporting deficiencies that weaken its scientific value and conclusions.

Major Comments

The primary weakness of this manuscript lies in its lack of scientific rigor and clear, evidence-based reporting. The central diagnosis of “anastomositis” is presented without a precise definition, leaving the reader to guess at its exact meaning. Is this a distinct pathological entity, or simply a descriptive term for inflammation? The authors fail to differentiate it from more common and well-understood causes of early postoperative obstruction, such as significant anastomotic edema, a small hematoma, or even a technical issue with the anastomosis that became clinically apparent with the introduction of oral intake. For this case to be a meaningful contribution, the authors must provide specific endoscopic and radiological criteria for their diagnosis. For instance, a detailed description of the endoscopic findings—such as the degree of luminal narrowing, the presence of friability, exudates, or ulcerations—is essential but conspicuously absent. Without this, the diagnosis remains speculative, and the term “anastomositis” is not a valuable addition to the clinical lexicon.

Furthermore, the treatment protocol employed is highly unconventional, and the authors do not justify its rationale. The administration of a pharmacological cocktail including high-dose corticosteroids, an antifibrinolytic agent (aminocaproic acid), a local anesthetic (novocaine), and adrenaline raises significant safety concerns. The use of high-dose dexamethasone in the immediate postoperative period is particularly alarming, as it is well-known to impair wound healing and increase the risk of infection and anastomotic leakage. An anastomotic leak is one of the most feared complications in bariatric surgery, and using a medication that could both increase the risk of a leak and mask its early signs (by suppressing the inflammatory response) is a dangerous proposition. The authors provide no evidence or logical basis for this specific combination of drugs, which appears to be an empirical and potentially hazardous approach. The manuscript would be substantially improved by a thorough discussion of the pharmacological rationale for each component of the treatment and a frank acknowledgment of the potential risks.

Another significant concern is the potential for conflict of interest and the appearance of self-promotion. The case was performed at the “Professor Oral Ospanov Surgery Center,” and the manuscript includes a citation to a biography of the senior author. Citing one’s own biography in a scientific paper is a departure from academic norms and, combined with the eponymous nature of the surgical center, creates an impression of bias that could undermine the reader’s confidence in the objectivity of the report.

Finally, the discussion of alternative diagnoses is critically insufficient. The authors do not adequately explore or rule out other possibilities for the patient’s symptoms. For example, could this have been a contained microleak that resolved spontaneously? Or was it simply severe anastomotic edema, which is a known cause of early dysphagia and often resolves with supportive care alone (intravenous fluids and bowel rest), without the need for the complex and risky pharmacological intervention described here? By not engaging with these alternative possibilities, the authors fail to make a convincing argument for the uniqueness of their diagnosis and the necessity of their specific treatment

Minor Critiques

Beyond the major scientific flaws, the manuscript suffers from several reporting and stylistic issues that detract from its professionalism and clarity. The title, “Case Report: Case report. Anastomositis on the 1st day after OAGB,” is not only redundant but also lacks the descriptive power expected of a scientific publication. A more informative title, such as “Conservative Management of Acute Anastomositis on the First Postoperative Day After One-Anastomosis Gastric Bypass: A Case Report,” would better capture the essence of the report and improve its discoverability.

Similarly, the abstract is presented as a single block of text. Adhering to a structured abstract format (e.g., Background, Case Presentation, Conclusion) is standard practice and significantly enhances readability for busy clinicians and researchers. The authors should also be commended for using the term “one-anastomosis gastric bypass (OAGB),” which aligns with current IFSO recommendations. However, they must ensure this terminology is used consistently throughout the manuscript, avoiding any lapse into the outdated term “mini-gastric bypass.”

From a clinical perspective, the report omits several key details that are necessary for a comprehensive understanding of the case. For example, the patient’s preoperative glycemic control (HbA1c), the specific medications used for his comorbidities, and any preoperative optimization strategies are not mentioned. These details are crucial for assessing the patient’s baseline risk profile. The follow-up period of only three months is also a limitation; while the short-term outcome is positive, longer-term data are essential to confirm the durability of the result and to monitor for any late-onset complications, such as the development of a true anastomotic stricture.

The manuscript’s language, while generally understandable, would benefit from a thorough review by a native English speaker or a professional editing service to correct minor grammatical errors and improve sentence structure. More critically, the reference list contains significant issues that undermine the scholarly quality of the work. Reference 5, a citation for Brethauer et al., is riddled with errors, including a misspelled author name (“Schauern” instead of “Schauer”), an incorrect journal abbreviation, and an incomplete page range.

Even more concerning is Reference 7, which is a citation for a biography of the senior author published in Obesity Surgery. This form of self-citation is inappropriate for a scientific article.

Novelty and Context within the Existing Literature

Some studies have described “anastomositis” in the context of OAGB, but these reports refer to a chronic inflammatory condition found during endoscopic surveillance years after the surgery. A notable example is the work by Felsenreich et al. (2023), which found anastomositis in over a third of patients at a mean follow-up of five years, likely related to chronic exposure to bile or other gastric contents [1]. The acute, fulminant presentation in this case report is a different entity entirely.

The novelty of this case, therefore, lies in its description of what appears to be a hyperacute inflammatory response at the anastomosis, and, perhaps more importantly, its successful resolution with a conservative, non-invasive medical regimen. In this case report, we see a patient with a confirmed diagnosis of severe obesity who underwent one anastamosis fundoring gastric bypass as the optimal surgical treatment method for this particular patient. The authors noted the patient's preoperative dyslipidemia and GERD, which significantly limit the choice of surgical method for this patient category. Therefore, a preliminary case description, examination data, and patient parameters are provided in full.

I am confident and convinced that the authors, in their discussion, have identified all possible solutions to the patient's condition, were able to understand and comprehend the cause-and-effect relationship in this case, find solutions to this situation, and, based on their reasoning, were able to formulate a correct conclusion. Given that the experimenters were unsuccessful in inducing sneezing in the lab by light stimulation one is led to wonder what the important differences between lab conditions and the conditions under which sneezing typically occurs.  These may be characterised as reflecting differences in the individual's physiology and differences in the light stimulation. As regards the individual's physiology, thermal comfort is one obvious difference between the natural and lab conditions. Sneezing is usually occasioned when an individual feels the cold, something they are more likely to do when outside than indoors. We are told that "Sneezing often took place during transitions between environments, e.g., walking from home to the bus station, or from the bus station to the workplace." Presumably the indoor temperature was stable and comfortable, unlike the conditions prevalent when sneezing occurred. Thermal instability is therefore a consideration.  There were also important differences between the light used in the lab and the daylight outside.  The multiLED source did not provide stimulation below 400nm.  It is possible that the UV present outdoors contributed to sneezing, given that Askenasy notes that keratitis has been reported to enhance the photic sneeze reflex.  If LB wears glasses this is unlikely to be an important concern given that CR39 lenses filter out most light below 380nm. If LB does not, however, there is the (admittedly remote) possibility that UV played a role.  Another indirect concern is that the light engine used pulse width modulation (PWM). Some individuals can discriminate steady from intermittent light at frequencies exceeding 15kHz.  Those that can do so tend to suffer eye-strain in everyday life. The intermittent light generates a spatial pattern during a saccade known (unfortunately) as the phantom array. It is remotely possible that the phantom array interfered in some way with eye movements or with appreciation of the bright light. If coloured fringes were visible during a saccade owing to the differences in PWM between the various LED sources, this would have been a distraction, if nothing more.
